Memorising is the easier half. Keeping it is the work of a lifetime.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, likened memorised Qur'an to a tethered camel: watch it and it stays, turn away and it is gone. Thabat is the tether — a short daily review that tests what you already carry, so that you keep carrying it.

WHY TESTING, NOT RE-READING

Pulling an ayah back from memory holds it more than twice as well as reading it again — for the very same minutes spent. It is also the older way. The Qur'an was carried by 'ard and mudarasah, recited back to someone who would catch you, never by reading in silence. Thabat is that someone on the days you cannot find one.

Have you ever memorized the Quran only to forget it later?

Many of us master pages of memorization early on, only to face a painful void months later — that heartache when you try to recall a verse and it's gone. This isn't a lack of willpower; it's simply how human memory works without structured review.

The Science of Forgetting

Psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus discovered that memory follows a predictable forgetting curve — and that reviewing at the right moment multiplies retention exponentially. Itqan applies this science specifically to the classical Islamic memorization methodology.
